questions.question_text:
A council wants to determine public opinion on building a new skate park.
They interview $200$ people entering a youth recreation centre on a Saturday afternoon.
Why is this sample unrepresentative of the whole municipality?

options.text: It uses convenience sampling at a single venue, heavily over-representing young active residents
The sample size of $200$ is too small for any municipal survey
options.why: The number 200 alone does not show whether a sample is adequate. The stated defect is selection at one venue rather than fair coverage of the municipality.

options.text: It relies on a stratified random design across suburbs
options.why: The method described is location-based convenience sampling, not stratified random sampling.

options.text: It violates ethical privacy rules by asking about recreational activities
options.why: The stem describes a biased selection location; asking about a skate park does not itself establish a privacy breach.

questions.solution_text:
People who do not attend this youth recreation centre at that time cannot be selected, and attendees may have different views from other residents.
It uses convenience sampling at a single venue, heavily over-representing young active residents.

questions.question_text:
A news website posts an online poll asking: 'Should Sunday trading hours be extended?' $5000$ readers vote.
Why cannot this sample be used to conclude what the general population thinks?

options.text: It is a self-selected sample covering only website visitors who chose to vote
The sample size of $5000$ is mathematically insufficient
options.why: The number 5000 does not correct the restricted coverage or self-selection. No rule about a minimum sample size is given.

options.text: The survey question is double-barrelled
options.why: The question asks a single simple question about Sunday trading hours.

options.text: The survey violates respondent anonymity
options.why: The stem does not say whether individuals can be identified. The stated problem is who could vote and who chose to respond.

questions.solution_text:
Only website visitors who choose to vote are included. Their views may differ from visitors who do not vote and from the wider population.
It is a self-selected sample covering only website visitors who chose to vote.

questions.question_text:
A national airline with $10\,000\,000$ annual passengers surveys $4$ passengers selected at random to evaluate passenger satisfaction.
Why is this a poor basis for representing passenger satisfaction?

options.text: The very small sample may miss much of the variety of passenger experiences
Random selection always produces biased results
options.why: Random selection does not systematically favour particular members. With just four passengers, however, the result may vary greatly by chance.

options.text: The airline used an unstratified quota system
options.why: The stem states passengers were selected at random, not via an unstratified quota system.

options.text: The survey questions must have been leading
options.why: The flaw is the tiny sample size, not the wording of the questions.

questions.solution_text:
Four passengers may miss much of the variety of experiences among the airline's passengers.
Random selection does not make such a small sample a strong basis for representing passenger satisfaction.

questions.question_text:
A researcher wants to estimate how many adults in a town can touch their toes. The researcher surveys $55$ adults attending a gymnastics class.
Why may this sample be unrepresentative?

options.text: Gymnastics participants may be more flexible than other adults in the town
Any sample containing $55$ people must be representative
options.why: This treats sample size as proof of representation and ignores the selection of only gymnastics participants.

options.text: The researcher has surveyed every adult in the town
options.why: This mistakes one gymnastics class for the whole population of adults in the town.

options.text: Choosing people from the same class guarantees the town's flexibility is represented
options.why: This assumes similarity within the selected group makes it representative, although adults outside the class are excluded.

questions.solution_text:
Only adults attending the gymnastics class are included.
They may be more flexible than adults who do not attend.
The sample may overestimate how common it is for adults in the town to touch their toes.

questions.question_text:
A researcher investigates Australian workers' travel to work by interviewing $170$ people at a railway station during the morning peak hour.
Why may this sample be unrepresentative?

options.text: It over-represents train users and misses workers who travel in other ways or work from home
Interviewing people during peak hour includes every Australian worker
options.why: This mistakes a busy station for complete coverage and ignores workers who are elsewhere.

options.text: All workers use the same method of travel
options.why: This assumes train passengers' travel represents everyone and ignores other ways of travelling and working from home.

options.text: The number of interviews removes the problem of surveying only train users
options.why: This assumes more interviews fix restricted selection, but workers who do not use the station remain excluded.

questions.solution_text:
The interviews include only people at the railway station at that time.
Workers who drive, walk, cycle or work from home are missed.
The sample may make train travel appear more common than it is among all Australian workers.

questions.question_text:
A researcher studies whether new cafés usually succeed by interviewing the owners of $85$ cafés that are still operating. Cafés that have closed are not included.
Why may this sample be unrepresentative?

options.text: It includes surviving cafés but excludes failed cafés, which may make success appear more common
Closed cafés are irrelevant when investigating whether new cafés succeed
options.why: This excludes the failures needed to judge success among all new cafés.

options.text: Interviewing $85$ owners guarantees that failed cafés are represented
options.why: This assumes sample size fixes an exclusion, although no closed cafés are included.

options.text: Every café that opens remains in business
options.why: This assumes there are no failures despite the question explicitly mentioning cafés that have closed.

questions.solution_text:
Only cafés that survived and remained open are included.
Closed cafés are missing from the sample.
This is survivorship bias and may make success appear more common than it is among all new cafés.

questions.question_text:
A telecommunications company surveys customer satisfaction by randomly generating landline telephone numbers.
Why does this method produce an unrepresentative sample of all mobile phone users?

options.text: It excludes mobile-only households, whose views may differ from those of landline users
Landline numbers cannot be selected randomly by computers
options.why: Computers can generate landline numbers at random, but doing so still excludes mobile-only households.

options.text: The sample size of landline calls is always too small
options.why: The issue is undercoverage in the sampling frame, not the quantity of calls made.

options.text: Telecommunications surveys violate commercial privacy regulations
options.why: No information about consent or handling personal data is given. The stated problem is that mobile-only users cannot be selected.

questions.solution_text:
Random landline calls cannot reach mobile-only households. Their views may differ from those of mobile users who also have a landline.
It excludes mobile-only households, whose views may differ from those of landline users.

questions.question_text:
Engineers inspect $160$ aircraft that returned from missions. The returning aircraft have many hits on their wings but few on their engines.
Why might a statistician recommend extra armour around the engines?

options.text: Aircraft hit in the engines may not have returned, so those cases are missing from the sample
Few engine hits on returning aircraft prove that engine hits are harmless
options.why: This ignores aircraft that did not return and treats evidence from survivors as evidence about every aircraft.

options.text: The most frequently damaged areas on survivors must always be the most critical areas
options.why: This confuses damage an aircraft survived with damage that may have prevented its return.

options.text: Inspecting $160$ returning aircraft guarantees that aircraft lost on missions are represented
options.why: This assumes sample size removes survivorship bias, although lost aircraft are still excluded.

questions.solution_text:
The sample contains only aircraft that survived and returned.
Aircraft hit in the engines may have been unable to return and would then be missing from the sample.
Few engine hits among survivors do not prove that engines are safe, so protecting them may reduce losses.
